content: Vaccines will be stored in passive containers, such as cold boxes, vaccine carriers, and coolant packs, for short periods during immunization campaigns when necessary. This approach depends on frequent and reliable vaccine distribution using effective transportation systems. The storage requirements for the Measles-Rubella Combination Vaccine (MRCV) specify that it must be kept between +2°C and +8°C. Once reconstituted, the vaccine must be kept on a reconditioned ice pack or in a foam pad and discarded after six hours or at the end of the immunization session, whichever comes first. Since the reconstituted vaccine lacks preservatives, it is prone to microbial contamination. Only the diluent provided by the manufacturer should be used for reconstitution, and this must be emphasized during training and supervision. Diluent interchangeability between different vaccines, such as monovalent measles, MR, and MMR, is not permitted. Reconstituted vaccines are less stable than their dry powder form and lose potency quickly, especially at room temperatures. For instance, at 22°C to 25°C, potency decreases by approximately 50% within one hour. Additionally, these vaccines are sensitive to UV light and must be protected from sunlight and kept cool. The introduction of MRCV is expected to have minimal impact on waste management if vial sizes and dosing schedules remain unchanged. However, provisions must be made for disposing of waste generated from additional routine vaccinations for women of reproductive age (WRA) and healthcare workers. Although the volume of waste is expected to be small and manageable, it is essential to verify that the current waste management system can handle any increase. Strengthening vaccine and healthcare waste management should be incorporated into comprehensive multi-year plans (cMYP) and vaccine introduction strategies. A communication plan must be developed before introducing any new vaccine, including the Rubella-Containing Vaccine (RCV). Adequate time should be allocated to assess community readiness, identify potential resistance or opposition, analyze causes of low coverage, and address these concerns with programmatic responses. Preparatory activities should include forming a communication committee, coordinating roles among partners, and gathering research and information to create an evidence-based communication strategy. Key messages should emphasize that the rubella vaccine is safe for children and adults, has been used successfully in many countries, prevents birth defects associated with rubella infection during pregnancy, and has no harmful effects when administered to pregnant women. The vaccine is typically given in combination with the measles vaccine as MR. Before introducing RCV into national immunization programs, healthcare workers must undergo training tailored to either supplementary immunization activities (SIAs) or routine immunization. For routine programs, a one-day training session covering background information, operational issues, and hands-on practice is sufficient. Training materials should be prepared in local languages and provided in adequate quantities. Job aids and summarized reference materials should be distributed to participants for future reference and sharing with colleagues. During training, it must be emphasized that MR vaccines should always be reconstituted using the manufacturer-provided diluent to avoid severe adverse events. Visual aids, such as pictures of the vaccine and diluent, can enhance understanding. Interactive and hands-on training methods, such as field visits, video demonstrations, and small group discussions, are more effective than passive lectures. Children entering primary school can be screened for missing immunizations, and any missed doses can be administered. If a child has not received MCV2, a dose of MRCV should be provided. If no prior measles vaccine has been given, two doses of MRCV should be administered at least one month apart. Collaboration with the Ministry of Education and private doctors is essential for screening vaccination histories and administering missed doses. Informed consent for vaccination must be obtained from parents or caregivers, following national regulations. Written consent forms, verbal consent, or implied consent protocols may be used, depending on the context. Supplementary Immunization Activities (SIAs) are critical for rubella and measles control or elimination plans. Initial wide-age-range SIAs aim to significantly reduce rubella virus transmission, thereby protecting WRA from infection and the risk of Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS). Monitoring and evaluation of routine RCV coverage are essential. Existing tally sheets, vaccination cards, and reporting forms must be updated to include RCV. Post-introduction evaluations (PIEs) should be conducted one year after introducing new vaccines to assess their impact on immunization systems. Rubella surveillance must be integrated with measles case-based surveillance. Rubella cases can initially be identified by testing sera negative for measles. Surveillance includes individual case reporting with laboratory confirmation and CRS surveillance at sentinel sites. Pregnant women exposed to rubella should be tested and followed until delivery to assess pregnancy outcomes. Susceptible women should be vaccinated after delivery. Laboratory testing for rubella-specific IgM and IgG is recommended for suspected cases. Pregnant women with confirmed rubella infection must be counseled and followed up to document pregnancy outcomes, which may include miscarriage, stillbirth, or CRS. CRS surveillance should be established as soon as possible after RCV introduction to monitor the vaccine program's effectiveness and detect affected infants. Surveillance systems should capture most suspected CRS cases, starting with sentinel sites and expanding over time.
